overview.what_it_is: This lesson develops the skills needed for two PTE Academic listening item types: Multiple-choice, choose single answer and Multiple-choice, choose multiple answers. In both tasks, the learner reads a prompt, listens to an academic recording once, identifies the requested information, evaluates the answer options against evidence from the recording, and selects the best-supported response or responses.

format_facts.label: Item types
format_facts.value: The lesson covers Listening: Multiple-choice, choose single answer and Listening: Multiple-choice, choose multiple answers.

format_facts.label: Preparation time
format_facts.value: There are 7 seconds before the recording begins. Use this time primarily to understand the prompt and identify the listening purpose.

format_facts.label: Audio playback
format_facts.value: The recording is normally heard once, so concentration, selective note-taking and recovery after missed information are essential.

format_facts.label: Single-answer response
format_facts.value: Only one option is correct. Select the option that best answers the exact prompt.

format_facts.label: Multiple-answer response
format_facts.value: More than one option may be correct. Evaluate every option separately and select only those supported by the recording.

format_facts.label: Prompt focus
format_facts.value: Prompts may test gist, detailed information, speaker purpose, organization, inference, attitude, feelings or degree of certainty.

format_facts.label: Note-taking
format_facts.value: Notes should contain brief key words, symbols and abbreviations rather than complete sentences.

scoring_factors.name: Answer accuracy
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the selected option or options correctly answer the question using evidence from the recording.

scoring_factors.name: Prompt control
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner responds to the exact demand of the prompt, including negative wording such as NOT, EXCEPT or LEAST.

scoring_factors.name: Evidence discrimination
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can distinguish relevant evidence from background details, examples, repetition and redundant information.

scoring_factors.name: Selection discipline
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner avoids unsupported choices, especially in multiple-answer items where unnecessary selections can reduce performance.

critical_rules: Read the prompt before thinking about the answer options.
Identify the listening skill being tested before the recording begins.
Underline or mentally emphasize negative words such as NOT, EXCEPT, INCORRECT and LEAST.
Use the 7-second preparation period mainly to decide what information you need to hear.
Do not try to write complete sentences while listening.
Do not stop concentrating because of one unfamiliar or unclear word.
Judge options by meaning and evidence, not by whether they repeat words from the recording.
For multiple-answer items, select only options that have clear support.
Keep your first evidence-based answer unless you notice a specific contradiction or misreading.
Answer the prompt, not merely the general topic of the recording.

learning_goals: Distinguish accurately between choose single answer and choose multiple answers instructions.
Recognize whether a prompt asks for gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference or stylistic information.
Use the 7-second preparation time to establish a clear listening target.
Take brief, selective notes using key words, abbreviations and symbols.
Identify main ideas and separate them from examples or minor supporting details.
Listen for specific facts, reasons, opinions, definitions and sequences when the prompt requires detail.
Infer a speaker's conclusion, attitude or degree of certainty from language, emphasis and context.
Recognize redundant or irrelevant information and exclude it from the decision.
Handle negatively worded prompts without accidentally selecting true statements.
Evaluate each answer option against evidence from the recording rather than relying on memory of isolated words.

core_method.name: TARGET–NOTE–MATCH
core_method.summary: Decode the prompt before listening, collect only information connected to that target, and then match each option to the strength and meaning of the evidence.

steps.detail: Confirm whether the task requires one answer or more than one answer. This determines how many options you may select and how carefully every option must be checked.
Classify the prompt as gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference or stylistics. Turn it into a simple listening question such as 'What is the main point?' or 'Why did the speaker mention this?'
Notice words such as NOT, EXCEPT, INCORRECT, LEAST or MOST. Restate the question positively in your own mind, for example, 'I need the mismatches.'
Predict the type of language that may answer the prompt. A reason question may contain because, since or therefore; an attitude question may contain clearly, unfortunately, perhaps or must.
Follow the whole recording but give extra attention to information related to the prompt. Do not attempt to record every detail.
Write content words, contrasts, causes, results, numbers, names and attitude markers. Use arrows, plus and minus signs, abbreviations and short phrases.
Compare each option with the recording's meaning. Accept paraphrases and reject options that are merely mentioned, exaggerated, reversed or unsupported.
Check that the number of selections matches the instruction and that every selected option directly answers the prompt.

core_method.formula: Instruction + Prompt skill + Key evidence + Option check = Supported selection

techniques.name: Prompt-to-skill decoding
techniques.purpose: To know exactly what kind of information must be extracted from the recording.
how_to: Read the full prompt before the audio begins.
Circle or mentally highlight the question word and any limiting expression.
Classify the demand as gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference or stylistics.
Rewrite the prompt mentally as a short listening target.
Keep that target active while listening.
techniques.example: Prompt: 'What is the lecture mainly about?' Listening target: 'Find the central message that covers the whole lecture, not one example.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Without a clear listening target, learners often collect random details and then choose an option that sounds familiar but does not answer the question.
techniques.common_error: Listening only for the topic noun, such as 'climate', without identifying what the speaker actually says about that topic.

techniques.name: Seven-second preparation priority
techniques.purpose: To use the short preparation period efficiently.
how_to: Read the instruction and prompt first.
Identify whether the answer must be single or multiple.
Mark negative or comparative words.
Predict the expected information type.
Read answer options only if time remains after the prompt is fully understood.
techniques.example: For 'Why does the lecturer mention steel?', the preparation goal is to listen for a function or reason, not simply every fact about steel.
techniques.why_it_matters: Trying to read a long prompt and all options within seven seconds can leave the learner uncertain about the actual question when the recording starts.
techniques.common_error: Scanning all answer options quickly but beginning the recording without understanding whether the prompt asks for a reason, opinion or main idea.

techniques.name: Compressed note-taking
techniques.purpose: To preserve useful evidence without losing attention to the recording.
how_to: Write content words rather than grammatical words.
Use abbreviations such as gov, env, edu, prob and sol.
Use symbols such as +, -, versus, arrows and question marks.
Record contrasts and cause-effect relationships.
Leave space to add a correction when the speaker changes direction.
techniques.example: Instead of writing 'Glass is used because it allows natural light into the building and weighs less than masonry,' write 'glass: light in + lighter than masonry.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Short notes reduce writing load and allow the learner to continue following the speaker's organization and emphasis.
techniques.common_error: Writing complete sentences, falling behind and missing the next important point.

techniques.name: Gist triangle
techniques.purpose: To identify the main idea rather than choosing an option based on one memorable detail.
how_to: Identify the general topic.
Ask what central claim or message the speaker makes about that topic.
Notice repeated ideas, opening statements and concluding statements.
Check which option covers most of the recording.
Reject options focused on only one example or detail.
techniques.example: Topic: urban transport. Central claim: cities should combine public transport with safe walking and cycling routes. A correct gist option must include the combined policy, not only bicycle lanes.
techniques.why_it_matters: Main-idea distractors frequently contain accurate details but represent only a small part of the recording.
techniques.common_error: Selecting the option that repeats the most recognizable words instead of the option that represents the whole message.

techniques.name: Detail checkpointing
techniques.purpose: To capture precise facts, reasons, definitions or sequences requested by the prompt.
how_to: Identify the category of detail required, such as why, when, where, how or how many.
Listen for names, figures, causes, results and examples connected to that category.
Write the requested detail beside a short label.
Notice corrections such as 'not X but Y' or 'initially, however'.
Compare options with the final meaning rather than the first statement heard.
techniques.example: Prompt: 'Why did the researchers repeat the experiment?' Note label: 'repeat why?' Evidence: 'first sample too small.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Academic speakers often introduce several facts, but only one fact answers the exact detail question.
techniques.common_error: Choosing a true statement from the recording that does not answer the question word.

techniques.name: Contrast and correction tracking
techniques.purpose: To detect the speaker's real position when an earlier statement is later qualified or corrected.
how_to: Listen for but, however, although, rather, instead, in fact and actually.
Mark the first idea briefly.
Add an arrow or correction when the speaker changes direction.
Give more weight to the final qualified position.
Check whether an option describes the initial idea or the speaker's final view.
techniques.example: Notes: 'online classes convenient BUT not equal access -> blended approach preferred.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Distractors often repeat the first idea heard, while the correct answer reflects the later contrast or conclusion.
techniques.common_error: Selecting an early statement and ignoring the speaker's later qualification.

techniques.name: NOT-prompt reversal
techniques.purpose: To prevent accidental selection of correct statements when the question asks for incorrect ones.
how_to: Mark the negative word before listening.
Restate the task as 'Find the false or mismatched options.'
Test each option against the recording.
Label supported options as true and unsupported options as false.
Select according to the negative instruction, not according to familiarity.
techniques.example: Prompt: 'Which options do NOT correctly match a material with its reason for use?' Select the material-reason pairs that conflict with or are not supported by the recording.
techniques.why_it_matters: Learners naturally look for correct information, so negative wording can reverse an otherwise accurate decision.
techniques.common_error: Identifying the true matches correctly and then selecting them despite the word NOT.

techniques.name: Option evidence audit
how_to: Ask whether the option directly answers the prompt.
Find the specific evidence supporting or contradicting it.
Check whether the option is too broad, too narrow or too absolute.
Reject options that use correct vocabulary but change the relationship between ideas.
For multiple answers, judge each option independently.
techniques.example: Recording: 'The policy may reduce congestion in some districts.' Option: 'The policy will eliminate congestion throughout the city.' Reject because 'may reduce' has been exaggerated to 'will eliminate'.
techniques.why_it_matters: Many distractors are partly true or use words from the recording while altering certainty, scope, cause or conclusion.
techniques.common_error: Choosing an option because one phrase matches the audio, without checking the complete meaning.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 1: Main Idea in a Single-Answer Item
worked_examples.input: Instruction: Select the correct response. Only one response is correct. Prompt: What is the lecture mainly about? Recording summary: The lecturer explains that urban trees cool streets, reduce storm-water runoff and improve residents' wellbeing. Although planting costs can be high, the lecturer argues that cities should treat trees as essential infrastructure. Options: A. The historical development of city parks. B. The difficulties of measuring rainfall. C. The importance of urban trees as city infrastructure. D. The most common species of urban tree.
worked_examples.decoding: The phrase 'mainly about' signals a gist question. The answer must cover the full recording, including the benefits and the lecturer's central argument.
worked_examples.plan: Note the topic, repeated benefits and final claim: 'urban trees -> cooling + runoff + wellbeing; essential infrastructure.' Reject options that mention topics not discussed or focus on one narrow detail.
worked_examples.model_answer: Select C: The importance of urban trees as city infrastructure.

annotations.comment: 'Mainly about' requires the central message, not an isolated fact.
Parks may be related to urban trees, but historical development is not discussed.
Storm-water runoff is mentioned, but rainfall measurement is not the lecture's focus.
This paraphrases the lecturer's overall argument and covers the recording broadly.
Tree species are not central and may not have been mentioned at all.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 2: Detailed Information in a Multiple-Answer Item
worked_examples.input: Instruction: Select all the correct responses. Prompt: According to the speaker, which benefits are produced by flexible working arrangements? Recording summary: The speaker states that flexible schedules can reduce commuting time, help some employees manage family duties and allow companies to recruit from a wider geographical area. The speaker warns that communication may become more difficult and does not claim that office costs always fall. Options: A. Employees spend less time commuting. B. Communication between colleagues becomes easier. C. Employees may manage family responsibilities more effectively. D. Companies can recruit candidates from more locations. E. Office expenses are always reduced.
worked_examples.decoding: The prompt asks for specific benefits, so each option must be checked against explicit supporting details.
worked_examples.plan: Create a benefit list: 'less commute; family duties; wider recruitment.' Mark communication difficulty as a disadvantage and 'always lower costs' as unsupported.

annotations.comment: Directly supported by the statement about reduced commuting time.
Contradicted because the speaker says communication may become more difficult.
Supported by the reference to managing family duties.
Supported by recruitment from a wider geographical area.
The absolute word 'always' is unsupported.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 3: Handling a NOT Prompt
worked_examples.input: Instruction: Select all the correct responses. Prompt: Which options do NOT correctly match a building material with its reason for use? Recording summary: Glass became popular because it is weatherproof, allows natural light into buildings and is lighter than masonry. Steel is valued because it can support tall structures while using relatively narrow columns. The speaker briefly mentions that skyscraper construction expanded after World War II. Options: A. Glass — allows natural light to enter. B. Steel — supports tall structures. C. Glass — became popular mainly because it was invented after World War II. D. Steel — is selected because it is transparent. E. Glass — can be lighter than masonry.
worked_examples.decoding: NOT reverses the normal task. The learner must identify incorrect material-reason matches rather than true matches.
worked_examples.plan: Write 'select false matches.' Check each pair: A true, B true, C false because the date is background rather than a reason, D false because transparency describes glass, E true.

annotations.comment: The required selections are the mismatches, not the accurate pairs.
It turns a historical date into a reason for glass use, which the recording does not support.
Transparency is associated with glass, not the structural reason given for steel.
The post-war reference is background information and should not be treated as the answer to a reason question.
A, B and E are accurate, so they must not be selected in a NOT item.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 4: Speaker Attitude and Degree of Certainty
worked_examples.input: Instruction: Select the correct response. Only one response is correct. Prompt: How does the speaker feel about the proposed university attendance policy? Recording summary: The speaker says, 'The proposal may improve attendance, but I am not convinced that compulsory monitoring is the right solution. It could place unnecessary pressure on students with work or family responsibilities. A trial might be reasonable, provided the results are reviewed carefully.' Options: A. Completely opposed and unwilling to consider any trial. B. Strongly certain that the policy will solve attendance problems. C. Cautious and doubtful, but open to a limited trial. D. Uninterested because the issue has no effect on students.
worked_examples.decoding: The prompt tests stylistics: attitude and certainty. Key signals include 'not convinced', 'could', 'might' and 'provided'.
worked_examples.plan: Note attitude markers: doubtful, cautious, conditional support. Reject absolute options because the speaker does not express complete opposition or certainty.
worked_examples.model_answer: Select C: Cautious and doubtful, but open to a limited trial.

annotations.comment: Shows doubt rather than strong support.
These modal verbs signal possibility and limited certainty.
Introduces a condition for accepting a trial.
Too absolute because the speaker is willing to consider a trial.
Accurately combines the speaker's reservations with conditional openness.

worked_examples.title: Worked Example 5: Speaker Purpose
worked_examples.input: Instruction: Select the correct response. Only one response is correct. Prompt: Why does the lecturer mention a failed medical trial? Recording summary: The lecturer is explaining why researchers must publish negative as well as positive results. The failed trial is used to show that unpublished failures can cause later researchers to repeat ineffective methods. Options: A. To criticize all medical research. B. To provide an example supporting the need to publish negative findings. C. To explain how the treatment was eventually commercialized. D. To compare hospital funding systems.
worked_examples.decoding: The word 'why' asks for the function of the example, not the factual details of the trial.
worked_examples.plan: Connect the example to the surrounding argument: failed trial -> hidden negative result -> repeated ineffective research -> publish all findings.
worked_examples.model_answer: Select B: To provide an example supporting the need to publish negative findings.

annotations.comment: Ask what argumentative job the example performs.
The failed trial illustrates a consequence of not publishing negative results.
This exaggerates a specific criticism into opposition to all medical research.
It accurately links the example to the lecturer's central argument.
Options C and D introduce topics not supported by the recording.

items.when_to_use: Use as a mental cue when the speaker explicitly introduces the central message.
Listen for a conclusion or interpretation following evidence or examples.
Use to identify a summary statement near the end of a section or recording.
Use when the speaker distinguishes the central issue from background information.
Use to capture the speaker's final position or overall message.
Recognize that the following information supports a broader point and may not itself be the main idea.
Listen for a precise fact, definition, number or case.
Use when the speaker narrows attention to an important supporting detail.
Use to identify examples belonging to a category.
Use to identify reported evidence, findings or statistics.
Expect a contrast, limitation or change in direction.
Listen for a concession followed by the speaker's more important point.
Use to distinguish the preferred or accurate idea from the rejected alternative.
Expect clarification, stronger evidence or correction of an assumption.
Record Y as the corrected or emphasized information.
Listen for a direct reason when the prompt asks why.
Listen for a conclusion or result based on earlier information.
Identify the consequence of a cause, policy, event or condition.
Identify the purpose of an action or recommendation.
Track a cause-effect connection that may be paraphrased in an option.
Signals strong confidence or emphasis.
Signals likelihood but not certainty.
Signals possibility and limited certainty.
Signals a negative evaluation or disappointment.
Signals doubt, reservation or disagreement.

items.item: Mentioned but not answering the prompt
items.when_to_use: Reject an option that contains true information but does not address the question.
Reject an option that extends the speaker's claim beyond the recording.
Reject an option that represents only one example when the prompt asks for the main idea.
Reject an option whose meaning is opposite to the speaker's statement.
Reject an option that sounds logical but is not stated or implied in the recording.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to read the prompt and every answer option during the 7-second preparation period.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The recording may begin before the learner has identified the actual listening target.
common_mistakes.fix: Prioritize the instruction, prompt type and key limiting words. Read options only if preparation time remains.

common_mistakes.mistake: Listening only for repeated words from the answer options.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Correct answers are often paraphrased, while distractors may repeat exact words but change the meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Match complete ideas, relationships and degree of certainty rather than isolated vocabulary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing full sentences while taking notes.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner falls behind and misses later evidence, contrasts or conclusions.
common_mistakes.fix: Use key words, abbreviations, arrows and symbols.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping mentally after missing one word.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Worry about one unclear part can cause several following ideas to be missed.
common_mistakes.fix: Leave a question mark in the notes and immediately continue following the speaker.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting a true statement that does not answer the prompt.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Multiple-choice questions test relevance as well as factual accuracy.
common_mistakes.fix: Ask, 'Does this option answer this exact question?' before selecting it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring negative wording such as NOT or EXCEPT.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner may correctly identify true information but select the opposite of what the task requires.
common_mistakes.fix: Mark the negative word and restate the task as 'select the false or excluded options.'

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a minor example as the main idea.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The selected option may be accurate but too narrow to represent the whole recording.
common_mistakes.fix: For gist questions, choose the option that covers the topic, central claim and overall direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating all information as equally important.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Background, dates, repetition and illustrations can distract from the evidence required by the prompt.
common_mistakes.fix: Label notes by function: main point, reason, example, contrast, result or background.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting every option that seems possibly correct in a multiple-answer item.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Unsupported selections reduce answer quality and may affect the score.
common_mistakes.fix: Require clear evidence for every selected option and leave doubtful options unselected unless the recording supports them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing an evidence-based first answer because another option sounds more sophisticated.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Complex wording can appear attractive even when it is unsupported or exaggerated.
common_mistakes.fix: Change an answer only after identifying a specific prompt error, contradiction or stronger piece of evidence.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: An option may change 'may help' into 'will solve' or 'some' into 'all', creating a false statement.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare certainty and scope words carefully, including may, might, often, sometimes, all, never and always.

common_mistakes.mistake: Deciding too early before the speaker finishes.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Later information may correct, limit or reverse an earlier statement.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep options provisional until the recording ends, especially after contrast markers.

time_budget.focus: Review the difference between single-answer and multiple-answer instructions, response rules and common prompt wording.
Classify prompts as gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference or stylistics.
Practise reading prompts, marking danger words and predicting the required evidence.
Convert spoken information into key words, abbreviations, symbols and relationships.
Distinguish main ideas from examples and capture requested supporting facts.
Identify why information is mentioned and infer speaker position or certainty.
Reject options that are unsupported, contradicted, too broad, too narrow or exaggerated.
Complete single-answer and multiple-answer items under realistic one-play conditions.
Identify whether errors came from prompt reading, listening, notes, inference or option evaluation.

drills.name: Prompt classification sprint
drills.instructions: Read ten prompts without audio. Label each one G for gist, D for detail, P for purpose, O for organization, I for inference or S for stylistics. Underline the exact words that reveal the category.

drills.name: Seven-second target drill
drills.instructions: Display one prompt for seven seconds. State the item type, listening skill, danger word and expected evidence type before the timer ends.

drills.name: Keyword compression drill
drills.instructions: Listen to 20-second academic statements and reduce each one to no more than six written content words plus symbols.

drills.name: Keep-listening recovery drill
drills.instructions: Use recordings containing unfamiliar terms. When an unknown word occurs, write a question mark and continue taking notes without pausing.

drills.name: Main idea versus example drill
drills.instructions: After a short recording, write one sentence for the main idea and list two supporting examples separately. Then reject options that represent only an example.

drills.name: NOT-prompt sorting drill
drills.instructions: For each negatively worded question, label options T for supported and F for unsupported, then select according to the negative instruction.

drills.name: Certainty ladder drill
drills.instructions: Order expressions such as might, may, probably, will and certainly by strength. Compare each recording statement with options that alter its certainty.

drills.name: Distractor diagnosis drill
drills.instructions: For every incorrect option, label the reason: not mentioned, opposite, too broad, too narrow, wrong relationship, wrong certainty or irrelevant detail.

drills.name: One-play timed set
drills.instructions: Complete a mixed group of listening multiple-choice items with each recording played once. Do not pause, replay or consult a transcript until all answers are submitted.

drills.name: Transcript evidence review
drills.instructions: After timed practice, use the transcript to underline the exact evidence for correct answers and mark the wording that makes each distractor incorrect.

practice_plan.routine: For every item, follow the same routine: confirm single or multiple answer, decode the prompt, mark negative wording, predict the evidence, listen once while taking compressed notes, compare options by complete meaning, select only supported responses, and review errors by category after practice.

mastery_checklist: I can distinguish immediately between a single-answer item and a multiple-answer item.
I can identify whether a prompt tests gist, detail, purpose, organization, inference or stylistics.
I can notice and correctly respond to NOT, EXCEPT, INCORRECT, LEAST and MOST.
I can use the 7-second preparation period without becoming distracted by long answer options.
I can convert a prompt into a simple listening target.
I can take notes using key words, abbreviations and symbols rather than full sentences.
I can continue listening after missing an unfamiliar word or unclear phrase.
I can identify a recording's main idea and distinguish it from examples.
I can capture requested details such as reasons, dates, results, definitions and sequences.
I can explain why a speaker mentions a particular example.
I can infer attitude and certainty from modal verbs, evaluative language, stress and context.
I can recognize contrasts, corrections and changes of direction.
I can dismiss redundant background information that does not answer the prompt.
I can reject options that are true but irrelevant to the question.
I can identify options that exaggerate certainty or scope.
I can evaluate every option independently in a multiple-answer item.
I can avoid changing an evidence-based answer without a clear reason.
I can complete mixed listening multiple-choice practice under timed, one-play conditions.
I can explain the evidence for every answer I select.
I can classify my errors and choose a specific drill to improve the weak skill.
strategy_notes: The prompt controls the listening process. Understanding the topic alone is not enough.
Preparation time should produce a listening target, not a complete reading of every option.
For gist questions, opening and concluding statements are useful, but repeated ideas across the recording are often stronger evidence.
For detail questions, label the requested category before listening, such as reason, date, result or definition.
For purpose questions, ask what function an example performs in the speaker's argument.
For organization questions, track movement such as problem to solution, cause to effect, past to present or claim to evidence.
For inference questions, combine clues without adding outside knowledge.
For stylistics questions, listen to qualifiers, modal verbs, evaluative vocabulary, stress and tone.
A familiar word match is weaker evidence than a complete meaning match.
An option can be factually true and still be wrong because it does not answer the prompt.
Absolute words such as always, never, completely and all should be checked carefully against the recording.
When the speaker says 'but', 'however' or 'in fact', the information that follows often carries greater decision value.
Historical dates and contextual facts may be redundant when the prompt asks for a reason or purpose.
In multiple-answer items, do not select an option merely because it is possible; select it because it is supported.
The best reason to change an answer is new evidence, not nervousness.
During review, study why distractors are wrong as carefully as why the correct answers are right.
